prompt.context: A major auto service chain, Wheeler Dealer, has enjoyed healthy returns on its 30-store operation for the past 10 years. However, management feels that the chain needs to expand, as the current geographical areas in which they are based have become saturated. For the past couple of years, they have aggressively pursued a growth strategy, opening an additional 15 stores. However, it seems that this approach has had negative returns. For the first time in over a decade, the chain's profits dropped into the negative zone.
prompt.question: You were hired to figure out why Wheeler Dealer's profits have dropped into negative territory despite its recent expansion.

clarifying_info.q: What type of services does Wheeler Dealer provide?
clarifying_info.a: There are two main businesses under each roof: off-the-shelf car parts (retail) and garage mechanical services.

clarifying_info.q: Are the same services offered in the newly opened stores?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, both businesses operate in the new stores as well.

clarifying_info.q: Have competitors entered the market and stolen market share?
clarifying_info.a: A few competitors have entered the market, but not too many. The expansion was planned to explore new markets and prevent competition from growing.

clarifying_info.q: Have prices changed to offset expansion costs?
clarifying_info.a: No, prices have stayed the same.

clarifying_info.q: Do the two business lines carry the same profit margin?
clarifying_info.a: No. Garage mechanical services cost the business more but command a premium price; the profit margin on garage services is twice that of off-the-shelf parts.

clarifying_info.q: Are the customers the same for both business lines?
clarifying_info.a: No. Garage service customers tend to come from a mid-to-high income bracket. Off-the-shelf parts customers tend to be lower-income and fix their own cars.

clarifying_info.q: Where has Wheeler Dealer traditionally been located?
clarifying_info.a: Mostly in, or very close to, the suburbs.

clarifying_info.q: Has the geographical location changed with the expansion?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. They saw certain urban areas as inexpensive and located more stores in inner cities where there are a lot of used car sales.

framework: Understand the nature of the business: two revenue streams — off-the-shelf car parts and garage mechanical services
Analyze customer segmentation: are the two streams serving different customers with different demographics?
Examine the profit structure of each offering: which has higher margin and why?
Investigate geographic shift: where are the new stores located and how does that differ from existing stores?
Apply the Profitability Framework: focus on how revenue mix has changed given the new locations

questions.prompt: What are the two business lines and how do their profit margins compare?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify the two distinct revenue streams — (1) off-the-shelf car parts retail and (2) garage mechanical services — and establish that garage services carry twice the profit margin of parts retail, due to higher-skilled labor and premium pricing.

questions.prompt: Who are the customers of each business line, and how does the new store geography affect customer mix?
questions.guidance: Garage service customers are mid-to-high income, suburban residents. Parts retail customers are lower-income, inner-city residents who self-repair. By expanding into inner cities rather than suburbs, Wheeler Dealer shifted its customer mix away from the high-margin garage service segment toward the lower-margin parts retail segment. The candidate should articulate that this mix shift directly explains the profit decline.

questions.prompt: Synthesize: why did adding stores lead to lower profits overall?
questions.guidance: The 15 new stores were placed in urban/inner-city areas that are demographically misaligned with the high-margin garage service business. The new stores disproportionately attract lower-income, self-service customers who buy parts but do not use the garage. Because the margin on parts is insufficient to cover total costs, total chain profitability turned negative. Prices were not raised to compensate.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options does Wheeler Dealer have to return to profitability?

categories.name: Geographic repositioning
ideas: Scale back from urban/inner-city locations and focus future expansion on suburban areas
Close or divest the worst-performing urban stores
Before opening new stores, screen locations by demographic profile (income, car ownership, DIY vs. service usage)

categories.name: Product/service mix adjustment
ideas: In underperforming urban stores, drop the garage service to reduce high fixed costs and focus purely on retail parts
Differentiate urban store format (parts-only) from suburban store format (full-service) to right-size cost structure

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Evaluate selective price increases on parts in urban stores if local competitive dynamics allow
Avoid broad price increases in price-sensitive inner-city markets

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce headcount of mechanics in stores that no longer offer garage services
Renegotiate leases on urban locations given lower revenue base

recommendation: Scale back from urban/inner-city areas and refocus expansion into suburban geographies where mid-to-high income customers will use the high-margin garage service
Where exit from urban locations is not immediately feasible, drop the garage service offering to cut costs and operate those stores as parts-retail-only outlets
risks: Exiting urban markets may involve lease break costs and write-offs
Downsizing to parts-only in some stores could reduce revenue if any garage demand exists
Remaining suburban expansion could still face saturation over time
next_steps: Audit each of the 15 new stores by revenue mix (parts vs. garage) and contribution margin
Identify stores that are structurally misaligned (high parts share, low garage utilization) and model closure or format conversion
Develop a site-selection criterion incorporating demographic data before approving future store openings
